bio.en: Karina Nguyen is a research engineer at Anthropic, where she works on the cutting edge of building and improving Claude, and previously did front-end engineering.
bio.zh: 卡琳娜·阮（Karina Nguyen）是 Anthropic 的研究工程师，在构建与改进 Claude 模型的最前沿工作，此前从事前端工程。

summary.en: Karina explains how her love of front-end engineering evolved into AI research as she realized models could build apps themselves. She argues that creative, aesthetic judgment is still hard to teach models and remains a key human skill. The episode demystifies how large language models are actually created and where human taste still matters most.
summary.zh: 卡琳娜讲述了她对前端工程的热爱如何随着"模型能自己构建应用"的认知而转向 AI 研究。她认为，创造性与审美判断仍难以教给模型，依然是人类的关键能力。本期揭开了大语言模型真实构建过程的神秘面纱，并指出人类品味在何处最为关键。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Not only are you working at the cutting edge of AI and LLMs, you're actually building the cutting edge.
turns.zh: 你不仅在人工智能和大语言模型（LLM）领域的前沿工作，更是在亲手打造这个前沿领域。

turns.speaker: Karina Nguyen
turns.en: When I first came to Anthropic and I was like, "Oh my God, I really love front-end engineering." And then the reason why I switched to research is because I realized, "Oh my God, Claude is getting better at front-end. Claude is getting better at coding. I think Claude can develop new apps."
turns.zh: 我刚加入Anthropic时，心里想：“天哪，我太喜欢前端工程了！”但后来转向研究的原因，是我意识到：“天哪，Claude在前端和编程能力上越来越强了。我觉得它能开发出新应用。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What skills do you think will be most valuable going forward for product teams, in particular?
turns.zh: 你认为未来对产品团队而言最有价值的技能是什么？

turns.speaker: Karina Nguyen
turns.en: Creative thinking and you kind of want to generate a bunch of ideas and filter through them and not just build the best product experience. I think it's actually really, really hard to teach the model how to be aesthetic or really good visual design or how to be extremely creative in the way they write.
turns.zh: 要有创造性思维，要能产出大量创意想法，再进行筛选，而不只是打造最佳产品体验。我觉得，要教会模型具备审美能力、出色的视觉设计能力，或者让它们在写作时展现极强的创造力，这实在太难了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What do you think people most misunderstand about how models are created?
turns.zh: 你认为人们对模型创建过程最容易产生哪些误解？

turns.speaker: Karina Nguyen
turns.en: When you taught the model, some of the self-knowledge of you actually don't have a physical body to operate in the physical world, the model would get extremely confused.
turns.zh: 当你教导模型时，一些关于你自身的知识——比如你没有实体身体在现实世界中行动——模型就会变得非常困惑。

turns.zh: 我很高兴您能来到这里，因为您不仅在人工智能和大语言模型领域处于前沿，还亲自参与了这些技术的研发。最近，OpenAI推出了首款代理功能，而您可能还不知道这件事。我对读者做了一项调查，询问他们日常工作中最常用的工具，ChatGPT高居榜首，领先于Gmail、Slack等所有工具。90%的人表示经常使用ChatGPT。

turns.speaker: Karina Nguyen
turns.en: That's quite good.
turns.zh: 这真是太棒了。两年前它还名不见经传。

turns.speaker: Lenny

turns.zh: 太不可思议了。两年前它还默默无闻。

turns.speaker: Karina Nguyen
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Also, we're recording this the week that OpenAI announced Stargate, which is this half trillion dollar investment in AI infrastructure. So there's just a lot happening constantly in AI and you have a really unique glimpse into how things are working, where things are going, how work gets done. So I have a lot of questions for you. I want to talk about how you operate and how you work at OpenAI, where you think things are going, what skills are going to matter more and less in the future, and also just where things are going broadly. So how does that sound?
turns.zh: 此外，我们这次录制节目时，OpenAI刚宣布了Stargate项目——这项价值5000亿美元的AI基础设施投资。所以AI领域的新进展层出不穷，而您对行业动态有着独特的洞察力。我有很多问题想问您。比如您在OpenAI的工作模式、未来发展方向、不同技能的重要性变化，以及整个行业的走向。您觉得怎么样？

turns.speaker: Karina Nguyen
turns.en: Sounds great. Thank you so much. Yeah, I was extremely lucky to join early days Anthropic and learned a lot of things there. And I joined OpenAI around eight months ago. So, yeah, I'm excited to dive more in into-
turns.zh: 听起来很棒。非常感谢您。是的，我很幸运能在Anthropic早期加入公司，在那里学到了很多东西。大约八个月前，我加入了OpenAI。所以，我很期待深入探讨——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, I'm going to definitely ask you about the differences between those, but I want to start more technical and just dive right in. I want to talk about model training. People always hear about models being trained, these big models, how much data takes, how long it takes, how much money toss it takes, how we're running out of data, which I want to talk about. Let me just ask you this question. What do you think people most misunderstand about how models are created?
turns.zh: 好的，我肯定会先从技术层面入手，直接深入讨论。我想先谈谈模型训练。人们总是听说模型训练需要大量数据、耗费大量时间、花费巨资，还面临数据短缺的问题，这些都是我想探讨的。首先我想问您，人们对模型创建过程最常误解的点是什么？

turns.speaker: Karina Nguyen
turns.en: Model training is more an art than a science. And in a lot of ways we, as model trainers, think a lot about data quality. It's one of the most important things in model training is like how do you ensure the highest quality data for certain interaction model behavior that you want to create? But the way you debug models is actually very similar the way you debug software. So one of the things that I've learned early days at Anthropic was we've discovered especially this Claude 3 training, when you taught the model some of the soft-knowledge of, "Hey, you actually don't have a physical body to operate in the physical world." But then at the same time you had data that taught the model some of the function calls, which is like, "This is how you set the alarm." (00:07:30): And so the model would get extremely confused about whether it can set an alarm, but it doesn't have a body in the physical world. So it's like the model gets confused and sometimes it'll over accuse. So sometimes it says, "Look, I don't know. Sorry, I cannot help you." And so there is always a balance trade off between how do you make the model to be more helpful for users, but also not being harmful in other scenarios. And so it's always about how do you make the model more robust and operate across a variety of diverse scenarios.
turns.zh: 模型训练更像是一门艺术而非科学。在很多方面，我们作为模型训练师，都非常关注数据质量。对于模型训练来说，最重要的事情之一就是如何确保为特定的交互模型行为提供最高质量的数据。但调试模型的方式实际上与调试软件非常相似。我在Anthropic早期就学到一点：特别是Claude 3的训练中，当你教会模型一些软知识，比如“嘿，你实际上没有身体在物理世界中行动”，但与此同时，数据又教会了模型一些函数调用，比如“这就是你设置闹钟的方法”。（00:07:30）于是模型会对自己能否设置闹钟感到极度困惑，但它又没有物理世界中的身体。所以模型会陷入困惑，有时甚至会过度指责用户。于是就需要在如何让模型对用户更有帮助，同时又不造成其他危害之间找到平衡。关键在于如何让模型更具鲁棒性，能够在各种不同的场景中正常运行。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is so funny. I never thought about that. Most of the data that it's trained on is kind of assuming it's like a human describing the world and how they operate. It assumes there's a body and you could do things, and the model is told you don't have a body.
turns.zh: 这太有趣了。我从没想过这点。模型训练所使用的大多数数据都是基于假设的，比如人类描述世界和他们的行为方式。这些数据假定模型有身体，可以执行各种操作，但现在模型被告知它没有身体。

turns.speaker: Karina Nguyen
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. I want to talk a little bit about data while we're on this topic. I know you have strong opinions here. There's this meme that models are going to stop getting smarter because they're running out of data. They're trained in a large part on the internet and there's only one internet and they've already been trained on it, what more can you show them about the world? And there's this trend of synthetic data, this term synthetic data. What is synthetic data? Why do you think it's important? Do you think it's going to work?
turns.zh: 好的。既然我们已经谈到了这个话题，我想再稍微聊聊数据。我知道你对此有很深的见解。有个梗说模型会停止变得更智能，因为数据已经用完了。它们在很大程度上是基于互联网训练的，而互联网只有一个，而且已经被训练过了，还能给它们展示多少关于世界的信息呢？现在有一种合成数据的趋势，合成数据这个术语。什么是合成数据？你为什么认为它很重要？你觉得它能行得通吗？

turns.speaker: Karina Nguyen
turns.en: I think there are two questions here. We can unpack one at a time. But people say we are hitting the data wall. I think people think more in the terms of pre-trained large models that are trained on the entire internet to predict the next token. But what actually the model is learning during that process is actually how do you compress the compression algorithm here? The model learns to compress a lot of knowledge and it learns how to model the world. So the next prediction of the word, like, "Teach me how to drive," basically. And you only have a few words that will match that, a car. So the model actually learns about the world in itself. So it's like it's modeling human behavior, sometimes it's modeling... And when you talk to pre-trained models which are very, very large, they're actually extremely diverse and extremely creative because you can talk to almost any Reddit user through a pre-trained model. (00:09:56): But I think what's happening right now with new paradigm of o1 series is that the scaling in post-training itself is not hitting the wall. And that's because basically we went from raw data sets from pre-trained models to infinite amount of tasks that you can teach the model in the post-training world via reinforcement learning. So any task, for example, how to search the web, how to use the computer, how to write, wow, all sorts of tasks that you trying to teach the model all the different skills. And that's why we're saying there's no data wall or whatever, because there will be infinite amount of tasks and that's how the model becomes extremely super intelligent. And we are actually getting saturated in all benchmarks. (00:10:52): So I think the bottleneck is actually in evaluations that we don't have all the frontier, like evals like, I don't know, GPQA, which is a Google-proof question answering, PhD level intelligence. The benchmark is getting to, I don't know, more than 60, 70%, which is what PhD gets. So it's literally hitting the wall in like evals.
turns.zh: 我认为这里有两个问题。我们可以逐一分析。但人们常说我们遇到了数据瓶颈。我觉得人们更多地从预训练大模型的角度来思考，即这些模型通过训练在整个互联网上的数据来预测下一个词汇。但实际上模型在此过程中学习的是如何压缩压缩算法？模型学会压缩大量知识，并学习如何建模世界。比如用户说"教我开车"，模型只能匹配到汽车这样的几个词汇。这说明模型本身在学习世界的本质。它在模拟人类行为，有时甚至能模拟……当你与非常庞大的预训练模型对话时，它们实际上极其多样且富有创造力，因为你几乎可以通过预训练模型与任何Reddit用户进行交流。（00:09:56）：但我认为目前O1系列新范式的情况是，训练后的扩展性不再受限。这是因为我们从预训练模型的原始数据集，转向了可以通过强化学习在训练后世界中教授模型的无限任务。例如，如何搜索网络、使用计算机、写作等各种任务。正因如此，我们才说不存在数据瓶颈，因为将有无限的任务，这也是模型变得极其智能的原因。我们在所有基准测试中都取得了显著成果。（00:10:52）：所以我认为真正的瓶颈在于评估方面。我们还没有达到所有前沿评估标准，比如GPQA（Google-proof question answering，谷歌级别的问答测试），要求达到博士级别的智能水平。目前最高只能达到60%、70%的准确率。这说明评估方面确实遇到了瓶颈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to follow both those threads. So the first is on this idea of synthetic data. Is a simple way to understand it, that the models are generating the data that future models are trained on and you ask it to generate all these ways of doing stuff, all these tasks as you described, and then the newer models trained on this data that the previous model generated?
turns.zh: 我想跟进这两个讨论点。首先是关于合成数据的概念。简单理解就是模型生成未来模型训练所需的数据，然后让新模型在这些数据上进行训练？

turns.speaker: Karina Nguyen
turns.en: Some tasks are synthetically curated. So this is an active research area is how can you synthetically construct new tasks with models to learn. Sometimes when you develop products, you get a lot of data from the product and user feedback and you can use that data too in this cross-training world. Sometimes you still want to use human data because actually some of the tasks can be really, really hard to teach. Experts only know certain knowledge about some chemicals or biological knowledge, so you actually need to tap into the experts' knowledge a lot. So yeah, I think to me synthetic data training is more for product... It's a rapid model iteration for similar product outcomes. And we can dive more into it, but the way we made Canvas and tasks and new product features for ChatGPT was mostly done by synthetic training.
turns.zh: 有些任务是经过合成策划的。这是一个活跃的研究领域，即如何利用模型合成新任务进行学习。有时开发产品时，会从产品和用户反馈中获取大量数据，并在这种交叉训练的环境中加以利用。但有时仍需使用真实数据，因为某些任务确实非常难教。比如专家对某些化学或生物知识有深入了解，所以必须充分借鉴他们的专业知识。是的，我认为合成数据训练更多用于产品……是实现相似产品成果的快速模型迭代。我们可以深入探讨，但我们开发Canvas、任务和ChatGPT的新产品功能，主要都是通过合成训练实现的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's actually get into that. That's really interesting. I want to talk about evals, but let's follow that thread. So talk about how this helped you create Canvas.
turns.zh: 让我们深入探讨这个问题。非常有趣。我想先谈谈评估问题，再跟进其他讨论。那么，请谈谈这如何帮助你们开发了Canvas。

turns.speaker: Karina Nguyen
turns.en: So when I first came to OpenAI, I really had this idea of, "Okay, it would be really cool for ChatGPT to actually change the visual interface but also change the way it is with people." So going from being a chatbot to more of a collaborative agent, and the collaborator is a step towards more genetic systems that become innovators ultimately. And so the entire team of applied engineers, designers, products, research got formed in the air almost out of nothing. It's just like a collection of people who just got together and we rapidly started iterating with each other. (00:13:46): Actually Canvas is one of the... I would say the first project at OpenAI, where researchers and applying engineers started working together from the very beginning of the product development cycle. And I think there's a lot of things that we have learned on the way, but I definitely came with the mindset of, "We need to do a really rapid model situation such that it would be much easier for engineers to work with the latest model possible, but also learn from user feedback or early internal dog food. How do we improve the model very rapidly?" (00:14:28): And it's really hard to kind of like figure out how people... when you deploy a product, how people would be able to use it. And so the way you synthetically train the model is physically figuring out what are the most core behaviors that you wanted the product feature to do. And for Canvas, for example, it came down to three main behaviors. It was how do you trigger Canvas for prompts like, "Write me a long essay," when the user intention is mostly iterating over long documents? Or, "Write me a piece of code," or when to not trigger Canvas for prompts like, "Can you tell me more about President..." I don't know, some of the general questions. So you don't want to trigger Canvas because the user intention is mostly getting answer, not necessarily iterate over the long document. (00:15:28): The second behavior is how do we teach the model to update the document when the user asks? So one of the behaviors that we taught the model is actually have some agency and autonomy to literally go to the document and select specific sections and either delete it or edit, so highlight it and rewrite certain sections. Sometimes the user would just say, "Change the second paragraph to be something friendlier," and we would have to teach the model to literally find the second paragraph in the document and change it to a friendly tone. So basically you teach both how to trigger edit itself, but also how do you teach the model to get higher quality edit for the document? (00:16:21): In case of coding, for example, there's also the question of how good the model is of completely rewriting the document, versus having a very specific target edits. So that's another layer of decision boundary within edit itself is, "Let's select the entire document and rewrite completely, or do you want to have a very targeted custom behavior." And when we first launched the model, we would bias the model towards more rewrites because we saw the quality of the rewrites were much higher. But over time you are shifting based on user feedback and what you're learning from iterative deployment. (00:17:02): Lastly, the third behavior that we taught synthetically the model is how to make comments on any document. So the way we used that is we would use o1 model to seem a way of user conversation, let's say like, "Write me a document about XYZ." But then we used o1 to produce the document and then we injected user prompt to be like, "Oh, make some comments, critique my piece of writing or critique this piece of writing that you just made." And then we taught the model to make comments on the document on very specific [inaudible 00:17:45] So it's also what kind of comments you want the model to make. Do they make sense or not? How do you teach the quality of that? And it all came down to measuring progress via very robust evals. But, yeah, this is how you used o1 and a synthetic data generation for the training.
turns.zh:
刚加入OpenAI时，我当时的想法是：“如果ChatGPT能真正改变视觉界面，同时改变与人类交互的方式，那会非常酷。” 因此，我们要从一个聊天机器人转变为更具协作性的智能体，而这种协作者是迈向更具创造力的系统的最初一步。整个应用工程师、设计师、产品经理和研究团队几乎凭空组建起来。这就像一群志同道合的人聚集在一起，迅速展开协作。（00:13:46）：实际上，Canvas是OpenAI的首批项目之一，在产品开发周期初期，就让研究人员和应用工程师从一开始就携手合作。我们在此过程中学到了很多东西，但我的初衷是：“我们需要快速迭代模型，让工程师能尽快使用最新模型，同时从用户反馈和内部测试中快速改进模型。” （00:14:28）：要理解用户如何使用产品实在不易。例如，当你部署产品时，用户可能希望用它来写长文案，但又可能只是在反复修改长文档。那么如何让Canvas准确识别这些意图呢？我们通过合成训练模型，找出最核心的用户行为。以Canvas为例，核心行为有三个：第一，当用户输入“写一篇长文案”时，如何触发Canvas？第二，当用户请求编辑文档时，如何教会模型更新文档？第三，当用户请求解释某个概念时，如何让模型准确理解上下文并进行智能编辑。（00:15:28）：第二个行为是如何教会模型在用户请求时更新文档。例如，我们教会模型自主选择文档中的特定段落进行删除或编辑。用户可能会说：“把第二段改得更口语化。” 这时模型需要准确找到文档中的第二段，并进行润色。（00:16:21）：在编程场景中，模型对完全重写文档的能力和针对性编辑的能力也需要权衡。这是编辑功能的另一个决策边界：是选择全文重写，还是针对特定需求进行定制编辑。最初我们更倾向于全文重写，因为重写质量更高，但随着用户反馈和迭代部署，我们逐渐调整策略。（00:17:02）：最后，第三个行为是教会模型在任何文档上进行注释。我们用o1模型模拟用户对话，比如“写一篇关于XYZ的文档”。然后用o1生成文档，并注入用户提示，如“把某段改得更口语化”。
用户：“请评论一下我的这篇文章，或者批评一下你刚刚写的这篇文章。”然后我们教会了模型如何针对特定文档进行评论[00:17:45，语音不清]。所以关键在于你希望模型做出怎样的评论。它们是否有意义？如何衡量其质量？这一切都归结于通过非常严格的评估来衡量进展。不过，确实如此，这就是如何将O1和合成数据生成用于训练的过程。

turns.speaker: Karina Nguyen
turns.en: It certainly depends on what you're developing, but there are various types of evaluations. Sometimes I do ask product managers, or there's also new roles that we have, model designers, to go through some of the user feedback maybe or think of various user conversations that should have triggered... Under these circumstances, it should trigger Canvas. And then you have this ground truth label of, "Okay with this conversation it should look trigger Canvas, under this conversation it should not trigger Canvas." And you have this very deterministic kind of eval that for decision-making behaviors is like this. (00:21:46): When we were launching tasks, for example, how do you make correct schedules is actually really hard for the model. But we built out some of the deterministic evaluations that is like, "Okay, if the user says 7:00 PM, the model should say 7:00 PM." So if you can have deterministic evals whether it's pass or fail. And the way it works is all the... Sometimes I ask product managers to just go create a double sheet, have different tabs and what's the current behavior, what's the ideal behavior and why, and some notes. (00:22:27): And sometimes they usually use it with evals, sometimes we use it for training. Because if you give the spreadsheet to o1 model, it can probably figure out how to teach itself a good behavior. And I think there are second type of evals that is more prevalent is human evaluations. And you can have specific trainers or you can have internal people to when you have a conversation of the prompt and then you have various completion of models, you choose the win rate. Which model is the best? Which model produce the highest quality comment or edit? And then you can have continuous win rates. And as you develop new models it should always win over the previous models. So it depends on what you want to measure.
turns.zh: 这当然取决于你正在开发的产品，但评估方式多种多样。有时我会请产品经理参与，或者让我们新设的模型设计师岗位，分析用户反馈或回顾可能引发问题的用户对话。在这种情况下，应该触发Canvas机制。然后你会给出一个标准标签，比如“基于这段对话应该触发Canvas”，“基于这段对话不应该触发Canvas”。这种非常确定性的评估方式，适用于决策行为的判定。（00:21:46）：比如我们在发布任务时，如何制定正确的时间表对模型来说确实很困难。但我们开发了一些确定性评估，比如“如果用户说晚上7点，模型就应该回复晚上7点”。所以你可以让评估结果分为通过或不通过两种。具体操作是，所有……有时我会让产品经理制作双列表，分成不同标签，记录当前行为、理想行为及其原因，并附上备注。（00:22:27）：有时这些表格用于评估，有时用于模型训练。比如把表格给模型，它可能就能学会正确的行为。我认为更常见的第二类评估是人工评估。你可以让特定培训师或内部人员，对比用户的提示内容和模型输出的结果，评估胜率。哪个模型表现最佳？哪个模型生成的评论或编辑质量最高？然后持续追踪胜率。随着新模型不断开发，它应该始终优于旧模型。总之，这取决于你想要衡量什么。

(00:44:47): And I feel like I see startups like Kaeser was doing super well. And that's because they iterate so fast. They invent new ways of training models. They move really fast. They listen to what users like, massive distributions. Yeah, it's kind of cool.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为创造性思维很重要。你需要生成大量想法，并进行筛选，而不仅仅是打造最佳的产品体验。倾听用户需求也很重要。你要开发出即使最通用的模型也无法取代的产品。很多时候，你开发出某个产品，为特定用户群体提供了极佳体验，但现在模型已经融入了用户反馈中。关键在于你是否善于倾听用户需求，是否能快速迭代。这些才是核心要素。我觉得我们尚未完全解决这个问题。目前有很多创意想法，我认为不必过于担忧。事实上，我觉得人工智能领域的人应该更具创造力，比如能跨领域整合不同领域的知识，开发出真正酷炫的新一代交互范式和人工智能应用模式。（00:43:53）：我认为我们根本没有攻克这个问题。几年前我曾告诉一些人，“要为未来而设计”。所以模型是否优秀、当前是否出色并不重要，但你可以构建产品理念，让模型在真正强大时能完美运作。我觉得这都是自然而然的结果。比如在Anthropic，Claude模型的输出……而Canvas早期阶段（2022年ChatGPT问世前），写作创意还只是我们的知识库[00:44:36]。但Claude 1.3模型本身并未达到极高编辑质量的标准，比如在编程领域。（00:44:47）：我觉得像Kaeser这样的初创公司做得非常出色。这是因为他们迭代速度极快，发明新的模型训练方法，行动迅速，善于倾听用户需求，拥有海量数据。确实很酷。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's really helpful actually. So what I'm hearing is that soft skills essentially are going to be more and more important, powerful. You just talked about management, leading people, being creative and coming up with innovative insights, listening. There's a post I wrote that I'll link to where I try to analyze how AI will impact product management. And we're actually very aligned, and my sense was the same thing, that soft skills are going to become more and more important. And the things that are going to be replaced is the hard skills, which is interesting because usually people value the hard skills like coding, design, writing really well. And it's interesting that AI is actually really good at that because it's taking a bunch of data, synthesizing it and writing, creating a thing, versus all these fuzzy things around of what influences, convinces people to do things and aligning and listening, like you said, creativity, anything along those lines come up as I say that.
turns.zh: 这真的很有启发。听你讲的，软技能将变得越来越重要、越来越关键。你刚刚提到的管理、领导力、创造力和创新思维，还有倾听用户需求。我写过一篇文章，链接给你，我试图分析AI将如何影响产品管理。我们观点非常一致，我的看法也是软技能将越来越重要。而被取代的将是硬技能，这很有趣，因为人们通常更看重硬技能，比如编程、设计、写作等。有趣的是，AI在这些硬技能上表现出色，它能处理大量数据、进行综合分析和生成内容，但在影响用户行为、说服用户做事、协调沟通、倾听用户需求等模糊领域，软技能反而更重要，正如你所说。

turns.speaker: Karina Nguyen
turns.en: I think it's actually a really, really hard to teach the model how to be aesthetic or do really good visual design or how to be extremely creative in the way they write. I still think ChatGPT kind of sucks at writing and that's because it's bottlenecked by this creative reasoning. I think characterization is one of the most important... I think for a manager, I feel like... (00:46:28): Actually, AI research progress is bottlenecked by management, research management. It's because you have constrained set of compute and you need to allocate the compute to the research paths that you feel the most convinced about. It was like you need to have a really high conviction in the research paths to put the compute, and it's more return on investment kind of situation. It's like, "Okay, I'm thinking a lot about across all my projects, which projects are higher priority?" Prioritization and also on the lower level, "Which experiments are really important to run right now and which are not?" and cut through the line. So I was thinking prioritization, communication, management. People skills like empathy, understanding people, collaboration. (00:47:23): I think Canvas wouldn't be an amazing launch if it wasn't about people and I think it's a wonderful group of people. And I get a chance to work with people like Lee Byron who's a co-creator at GraphQL and some of the best Apple designers. It's so cool to see... and how do you create this collaboration between people. It's just something that's still humane, I think.
turns.zh: 我认为，要教会模型具备审美能力、出色的视觉设计能力，或者在写作方面极具创造力，其实真的非常、非常困难。我仍然觉得ChatGPT在写作方面表现不佳，原因在于它受限于创造性推理的瓶颈。我认为角色塑造是最重要的……对管理者而言，我觉得……（00:46:28）：实际上，人工智能研究的进展受限于管理层，特别是研究管理层。这是因为计算资源有限，你需要将计算资源分配到你最有信心的研究路径上。你必须对研究路径有极高的信心才会投入计算资源，这更像是一种投资回报率的考量。比如，你需要在所有项目中仔细思考哪些项目优先级更高？优先级排序，以及在更细微的层面上，哪些实验现在必须开展，哪些可以暂缓？从而筛选出重点项目。所以我认为优先级排序、沟通和管理很重要。人际交往技能，比如同理心、理解他人、合作能力等也很重要。（00:47:23）：我觉得如果Canvas不是一个以人为本的产品，它就不会如此成功。我认为这是一个很棒的团队。我有机会与Lee Byron这样的人合作，他是GraphQL的共同创造者，还有一些苹果公司的顶尖设计师。看到他们之间的合作真是太棒了……而如何在人与人之间建立这种协作关系，仍然是需要人性化处理的事情，我认为。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me just follow through a little bit. I imagine people listening are like, "Okay, but once we have AGI or SGI it's like it'll do all this." There's a world where like, "Why isn't all this done?" I think it's easy to just assume all that. I'm curious this idea of creativity and listening, why you think AI isn't good at it, other than it's just very hard to train it to do this well. Is there anything there of just why this is especially difficult for AI and LLMs to get good at?
turns.zh: 让我稍微展开一下。我能想象听众会想：“好吧，但一旦我们拥有通用人工智能（AGI）或强人工智能（SGI），它就能处理所有这些问题了。” 但总有人会问：“为什么这些问题还没被解决呢？” 我觉得人们很容易就想当然地认为所有这些问题都能被解决。我很好奇你提到创造力和倾听能力，为什么你认为AI在这方面不擅长，除了训练它做好这件事太难之外？还有其他什么原因让AI和大语言模型（LLM）在这些方面特别难以做到出色？

turns.speaker: Karina Nguyen
turns.en: I think currently it's difficult for many reasons. I think it's still an active research area and it's something that I think my team is working on. It's like, "Okay, how do we teach the models to be more creative in the writing?" And so I'm thinking this new paradigm of wise that the models think more should actually lead to better writing in itself. But when it comes down to idea generation or discriminating of what is a good visual design or not, I feel like it hasn't had learned examples from people to discriminate it very well. I do think it's because there are not that many people who are actually really... It's not accessible to models to learn from these people I guess. So I definitely think that's why it sucks.
turns.zh: 我认为目前有很多原因导致这很困难。我认为这仍然是一个活跃的研究领域，也是我的团队正在努力攻克的难题。比如，“如何教会模型在写作中更具创造力？” 我认为新的范式——让模型更多地思考——本身应该能带来更好的写作效果。但当涉及到创意生成或判断一个设计是否优秀时，模型还没有从人类身上学习到足够的例子来准确判断。我确实认为这是因为真正具有创造力和审美能力的人太少了。我猜模型无法从这些人身上学习，所以我确实认为这很糟糕。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, that makes sense. Basically there's not enough of you yet, researchers teaching it to do these things, slash people that have incredible taste and creativity that can teach these things. You could argue this will come.
turns.zh: 是的，这说得通。基本上就是现在研究者太少了，没人教它做这些事，或者说有创造力和审美能力的人太少了，没人教它这些。你可以说这些问题会逐渐解决的。

turns.speaker: Karina Nguyen
turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: But we don't need to keep going down that thread. Let me ask you a specific question. In this post I wrote, I made this argument that a lot of people disagreed with that strategy is something that AI tooling will become increasingly great at and take over. There's the sense that that's the thing that people will continue to be much better at and you can't offload to AI basically developing your strategy, telling you what to do to win. My case is, "Isn't strategy, just take all the inputs, all the data you have available, understand the world around you and come up with a plan to win?" It feels like AI and LLM would be incredibly smart at this. What's your take?
turns.zh: 不过我们没必要再继续讨论这个话题了。让我问你一个具体的问题。在我写的这篇帖子中，我提出了一个观点：许多人不认同这样一种策略——即让AI工具变得越来越擅长接管这项工作。人们总觉得，制定策略仍然是人类最擅长的事情，你不能把制定策略、告诉你如何取胜的任务外包给AI。我的观点是，"策略不就是综合所有输入、利用现有数据、理解周围环境，然后制定获胜计划吗？"我觉得AI和大语言模型在这方面会非常出色。你怎么看？

turns.speaker: Karina Nguyen
turns.en: I think so too. I think again, you teach the model all sorts of tools and capabilities and reasoning and it's like when it comes down to... For Canvas right now, it would be very cool for the model just aggregate all the feedback from users, summarize me the top five most painful flows on user experiences. And then the model itself is very capable of thinking of knowing how it's been made, figure out how to create a dataset for itself to train on it. And I don't think that we are far away from that self-improvement, models becoming self-improved by... (00:50:54): That, and the part of development, is basically self-improving. It's kind of like its own organism or something. Again, like strategies, it's more like data analysis and coming up with... I think what models are really good at is connecting the dots, I think. It's like if you have user feedback from this source, but you also have an internal dashboard with metrics and then you have other feedback or input and then it can create a plan for you, recommendations even. And I think this is one of the most common use cases for ChatGPT too, is coming up with these sort of things.
turns.zh: 我也这么认为。我觉得，再次强调，当你教给模型各种工具、能力和推理能力时，当涉及到……就拿Canvas来说，如果模型能汇总用户的所有反馈，给我总结用户体验中最痛苦的五个流程，那就太棒了。而且模型本身就非常善于思考——它能了解自己的构建方式，知道如何为自己创建数据集用于训练。我觉得我们离模型自我改进不远了，模型会逐渐自我提升……（00:50:54）：还有开发部分，本质上也是自我改进。它就像一个自组织的实体。回到策略层面，更多的是数据分析和方案制定。我认为模型真正擅长的是连接各个点，比如你从这个来源获得用户反馈，同时你还有一个内置的指标仪表盘，然后再加上其他反馈或输入，它就能为你制定计划，甚至给出建议。这也是ChatGPT最常见的用例之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That makes sense essentially a human can only comprehend so much information at once and look at so much data at once to synthesize takeaways. And as you said, these context windows are huge now. Here's all the information, what's the most important thing I should do?
turns.zh: 确实，人类一次只能理解和处理有限的信息量。正如你所说，这些上下文窗口现在非常大。所有信息摆在面前，最重要的是我该做什么？

turns.speaker: Karina Nguyen
turns.en: Yeah, same as scientific research. Ideally the model would be able to suggest ideas, new ideas, or iterate on the experimental given the empirical results of the previous experiments like how do you come up with new ideas or the methods?
turns.zh: 是的，和科学研究一样。理想情况下，模型应该能够根据之前实验的实证结果，提出新想法或迭代实验方案，比如如何产生新想法或方法？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Oh, man. Okay, so just to close the loop on this conversation, this part of the thread is the skills you're suggesting people focus on building and leaning into is soft skills like creativity, managing influence, collaboration, looking for patterns. Is that generally where your mind is at?
turns.zh: 是的。天啊。所以来总结一下这段对话，这个讨论的核心是，你建议人们应该专注培养的技能是软技能，比如创造力、影响力管理、协作、寻找模式。总的来说，你的关注点在这些方面吗？

turns.speaker: Karina Nguyen
turns.en: Yeah, I'm thinking a lot about how do we make organizations more effectively and I think this is mostly management, I guess. It's like how do you organize research teams or generally teams combined... Compose teams such that they will be at their maximally succeed or at the maximal performance of what can possibly... We can literally create the next generation of computers. It's just the matter of conviction and the way you manage through that. It's scaling organizations or scaling product research, I guess.
turns.zh: 是的，我一直在思考如何让组织更高效，我觉得这主要涉及管理层面吧。比如如何组织研究团队，或者更广泛地说，如何组建团队……组建一个能最大限度地成功或发挥潜力的团队……我们甚至可以创造下一代计算机。关键在于信念和管理方式。无论是扩展组织规模还是产品研究，我想都是如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I think you're basically building this thing and not efficiently doing it is limiting the potential of the human species right now.
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得你们目前正在构建的这个系统，如果效率不高，就会限制人类物种的潜力。

turns.speaker: Karina Nguyen
turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's mismanagement within the research team in OpenAI and Anthropic and some of these other models.
turns.zh: 这是OpenAI和Anthropic等研究团队内部管理不善的问题。

turns.speaker: Karina Nguyen
turns.en: Yeah, it's kind of crazy to think about it.
turns.zh: 是啊，一想到这事儿就觉得挺不可思议的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Holy moly. Okay, so speaking of Anthropic and OpenAI, you've worked at both. Very few people have worked at both companies and have seen how they operate. I'm curious just what you've noticed about the differences between these two, how they operate, how they think, how they approach stuff. What can you share along those lines?
turns.zh: 天哪。说到Anthropic和OpenAI，你在这两家公司都工作过。在这两家公司工作过并了解其运作方式的人很少。我很好奇你观察到这两家公司在哪些方面存在差异，比如运营方式、思维模式、处理问题的方式等等。能否分享一下你的见解？

turns.speaker: Karina Nguyen
turns.en: It's more similar than different. Obviously there was a lot of... There are some differences always comes to nuances. I would say culture. I really love Anthropic and I have a lot of friends there. And I also love OpenAI and they still have a lot of friends though. So it's not about enemies. I feel like there's in AI, it's all like, "Yeah, they're competitors. There's enemies." It's actually like one big community of people doing the same thing. I would say what I've learned from Anthropic is this real care and craft towards model behavior, model craft, model training. (00:54:32): And I've been thinking a lot about, "Okay, what makes Claude Claude and what makes ChatGPT ChatGPT?" And it's like I still have some sense of operational processes that leads to the outputs, to the model. It's the outputed model. And it's like the reason why Claude has so much more personality and is more like a librarian... I don't know. I don't know. I am visualizing Claude being like a librarian at some point, very nerdy or something. ... is because I feel like it's the reflection of the creators who are making this model. And a lot of details around the character and the personality and whether the model should follow up on this question or not. (00:55:19): What's the correct ethical behavior for the model in these scenarios? A lot of crafts and curated datasets. This is where I learned that part of art, I guess, at Anthropic. I would say Anthropic is much smaller. When I joined it was, what, like 70 people? When I left it was tons of people. And obviously the culture changed so much. I really enjoyed being early days startup lives, and people knew each other as a family. But the culture shifted. (00:55:53): I would say that I learned from Anthropic that they're much better at focusing and prioritization of... Very hardcore prioritization, I guess. And they need to do it. But I think OpenAI's much more innovative and much more risk-takers in terms of product or research. Actually, in way your full-time job can be just teaching the model how to be creative writers. And it's like there's some luxury in this research freedom that comes with scale, maybe. I don't know. I'd say I have much more creative product freedom to do almost anything, I guess, within OpenAI, evolve ChatGPT into the vision that we want. It's more probably bottoms-up, I guess.
turns.zh: 它们的相似之处多于不同之处。显然存在一些细微差别，比如文化差异。我真的很喜欢Anthropic，在那里有很多朋友。不过我也喜欢OpenAI，那里也有很多朋友。所以这不是敌对关系。在AI领域，人们总说"他们是竞争对手，是敌人"，但实际上这是一个共同体，大家都在做同样的事情。我从Anthropic学到的是对模型行为、模型训练的精心打磨。（00:54:32）：我一直在思考，"是什么让Claude成为Claude，ChatGPT成为ChatGPT？"我觉得这和操作流程有关，最终决定模型的输出。模型本身的输出很重要。比如Claude为什么有更强的个性，像个图书管理员……我不知道。我能想象Claude在某些时候像个书呆子……这可能是因为模型创造者的个人风格所致。比如角色性格的设定，模型是否应该回应某个问题等细节。（00:55:19）：在这些场景中，模型的正确伦理行为是什么？这需要大量精细打磨和精心挑选的数据集。这也是我在Anthropic学到的艺术部分。我得说Anthropic规模小得多。我加入时大概只有70人，离开时人数激增，文化也发生了巨大变化。我很享受初创公司的早期生活，同事们亲如一家。但文化变了。（00:55:53）：我从Anthropic学到的是，他们更善于专注和优先处理事务……我想说他们非常注重优先级划分，而且必须做到这一点。但OpenAI在产品或研究方面更具创新性和冒险精神。实际上，在OpenAI，全职工作可能就是教模型如何成为创意作家。这里或许有规模带来的研究自由度，我不知道。我觉得在OpenAI，我有更大的创意产品自由度，可以几乎无拘无束地把ChatGPT发展成我们理想中的模型。可能更像是自下而上的发展。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, that's how I was thinking about it. It feels like OpenAI is more bottoms-up, distributed, people bubble up ideas, try stuff. And that leads to more products launching, I imagine more things just kind of being tried versus more of a, "Let's just make sure everything we do is awesome and great and craft and thinking deeply about every investment."
turns.zh: 是啊，我之前就是这么想的。OpenAI 似乎更注重自下而上、分布式开发，人们会不断涌现创意，尝试各种新方案。这也促成了更多产品的推出，我想相比于那种“确保我们做的一切都完美无缺、精心打磨、深思熟虑每个投资决策”的模式，这里更多的是去尝试新事物。

turns.speaker: Karina Nguyen
turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's really interesting. I've never heard it described this way. Karina, we've covered so much ground. This is going to help a lot of people with so many ways of thinking about where the future's going. Before we get to our very exciting lightning round, I'm curious if there's anything else that you think might be helpful to share or get into?
turns.zh: 这真的很有趣。我从未听过这样的解读。卡琳娜，我们已经探讨了这么多内容。这对许多人思考未来发展方向会有很大帮助。在我们进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，我很好奇你是否还有其他值得分享或深入探讨的见解？

turns.speaker: Karina Nguyen
turns.en: One of my regrets, I guess, when I was early days at Anthropic was that... I think there was some luxury of the time, because pre-ChatGPT, to actually come in with a bunch of ideas and prototype almost every day. And I think that we did a lot of cool ideas like Claude, and Slack was actually one of the first tool-usey products. It's like Claude could operate in your workplace now. It's kind of cool because you can add Claude to summarize the thread. So maybe you have an entire conversation with someone and then you want a summary of what happened you can ask Claude, "Summarize this." (00:58:07): Also, it was really fun to iterate on the model itself. It's like when you just talk to the model in Slack forever. It created some social element, it was kind like [inaudible 00:58:19] and this Discord, people learned so much about prompting and how to work with Claude. Actually, one of the features that was early tasks prototype is every Monday Claude would just summarize the entire channel. Or every Friday we'd just summarize a bunch of channels and give the news about the organization, or something. (00:58:48): And it's kind of like really cool form factor. I think thinking about form factor's a really important question in AI, especially we haven't even figured out how do we create an awesome product experience with o-series models. It's like the paradigm between synchronous real time give an answer paradigm into more asynchronous paradigm of agents working on the background. But then now the question is the agents should build trust with you, right? And trust builds over time, which is like with humans. And you start this collaboration which is why this collaboration model with you and the model is so important because you build trust and the model learns from your preferences so that it can become more personalized and it will start predicting the next action that you want to take on the computer or something. And it's more predictive, much more... We went from personal computers to personal model basically here.
turns.zh: 我觉得我在 Anthropic早期阶段的一个遗憾是……当时因为 ChatGPT 之前的技术限制，我们有更多时间去尝试各种想法，几乎每天都在做原型测试。比如我们开发了 Claude 这样的产品，Slack 也是最早的工具型产品之一。现在 Claude 甚至可以应用于职场场景——你可以在 Slack 里添加 Claude 来总结对话内容。这真的很酷，因为你可以让 Claude 总结整个对话流程。（00:58:07）此外，迭代模型本身也非常有趣。比如在 Slack 里不断与模型对话时，会产生社交互动效应，人们在 Discord 里学习如何设置提示语、如何与 Claude 协作。实际上，早期原型中的一个功能是每周一让 Claude 总结整个频道内容，或者每周五汇总多个频道信息并发布组织动态等。这确实是一种很酷的交互方式。我认为思考交互形式在人工智能领域非常重要，尤其是我们至今还没弄清楚如何利用 O-Series 模型打造出卓越的产品体验。比如从同步实时回答范式，转向更异步的智能体后台处理范式。但现在的问题是，智能体需要与用户建立信任，对吧？信任是随着时间建立的，就像人与人之间的信任一样。这种协作模式至关重要，因为信任能让模型学习你的偏好，从而实现个性化推荐，预测你的下一步操作。比如从个人电脑时代到个人模型时代的转变。

turns.zh: 我觉得Claude和Slack的形态在你想谈论新功能时受到了一定的限制。

turns.en: Bummer. I want that.
turns.zh: 真可惜。我想要那个功能。

turns.zh: 我知道ChatGPT有Slackbar工具。但我不知道，也许它会再次回归。

turns.en: I think the very first launch when we felt... turns.zh: 我认为最初的发布时，我们感到……当用户点击时，当时的模型只能处理10万个上下文的窗口。也就是说，用户可以上传一本书，让模型总结书的内容，或者处理财务报告之类的多文件内容，然后回答具体的问题。我觉得当时有一种感觉，"天哪，这真是一个很酷的新功能。"这不是模型的能力，而是产品形态本身带来的功能改进，而不是模型本身的进步。（01:01:34）：我们当时还考虑过其他原型……有一个Claude工作区的主意，类似于Claude的概念，我们可以共享一个文档工作区，用户可以在文档中进行迭代。但有时候这些想法会被搁置两年，就像这次的情况一样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting, there's these milestones that kind of open up our view of what is happening and where things are going. turns.zh: 很有趣的是，这些里程碑会打开我们的视野，让我们看到正在发生什么，未来会走向哪里。ChatGPT是第一个真正让人惊叹的东西，"哇，这比我想象的要好得多"。你提到10万个上下文的窗口，你可以上传一本书并提问，让模型总结内容。我现在经常用这个功能。当我采访嘉宾时，他们写了一本书，但我没有时间读完整本书，所以我用这个功能帮助我理解最有趣的部分，然后再去仔细阅读整本书。还有语音功能，你可以和ChatGPT对话。还有其他哪些时刻让你感叹，"天哪，这比我想象的要好得多？"

turns.zh: 这是一个推广Lennybot的好机会，让它加入进来。它已经在我所有的播客和新闻通讯上进行了训练。

turns.speaker: Karina Nguyen
turns.en: Much of it is because right now the model's operating on pixels instead of language or whatnot. Pixels is actually really, really hard.
